Key data types like DATETIME (for check-in/out), DECIMAL (for rates), and BOOLEAN (for availability) are critical because they ensure precise, real-time inventory management and accurate financial transactions. Furthermore, by analyzing numerical booking data (e.g., length of stay, guest count) against Boolean availability flags, I can implement dynamic pricing, allowing the system to automatically adjust rates during high-demand periods to maximize revenue.

A dinner reservation system allows different types of users to interact with the same system in different ways. Diners use the system to choose an available time slot and party size, and then submit a reservation request. The system collects this information and checks it against the restaurant’s available settings. Restaurant owners or administrators control the available time slots and allowed party sizes. When an owner changes these settings, it directly affects what options diners can see and select. For example, if a time slot is removed by the owner, diners can no longer reserve that time. Similarly, when a diner books a reservation, it reduces availability for other diners. This shows how actions by one type of user can impact the experience and options of other users in the reservation system.

Some of the data collected is important because it allows the reservation system to function accurately and efficiently. For example, collecting a diner’s email address and phone number allows the system to send confirmations, reminders, and cancellation notifications. Owner and staff data such as available time slots and table capacity help prevent overbooking and scheduling conflicts. Overall, this data improves communication between users and ensures reservations are handled correctly.

If there is only one table available and diner 1 successfully books it, the system should immediately mark the table as unavailable. When diner 2 attempts to book the same table, the system should prevent the booking and display a message indicating that the table is no longer available. This prevents double-booking and keeps reservation data accurate.

The system should assign tables based on party size to best fit the diners’ needs. The diner with a party size of two should be assigned the two-person table, and the diner with a party size of four should be assigned the four-person table. This ensures efficient use of space and allows both reservations to be accommodated whenever possible.
